sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: Agaricus campestris has a white to cream, domed cap, usually about 3–11 cm wide, that broadens with age. Its crowded free gills are pink on opened young specimens and turn reddish brown, then dark chocolate brown. A thin ring on the short white stem often collapses or disappears. The stem base has no membranous cup. The spore print is dark chocolate brown.

sections.title: Flesh, habitat and season
sections.text: The thick white flesh does not bruise bright yellow, including at the stem base; an occasional faint pinkish tinge is possible. The odour is pleasantly mushroom-like rather than sharply chemical. It grows in meadows, pastures and lawns, often in autumn. Do not rely on grassy habitat to establish identity.

sections.title: Dangerous confusions
sections.text: The poisonous Agaricus xanthodermus can resemble it closely and also has pink gills, but scratches or cuts quickly stain bright yellow, especially in the stem base, and its odour is often phenolic or disinfectant-like. Deadly white Amanita species have white gills and a white spore print; a volva may be buried around their stem base. Very young closed buttons may not expose enough characters for safe identification.

sections.title: Food safety
sections.text: A. campestris is listed as edible by mycological authorities, but a drawing or one character is insufficient. Examine each fully opened specimen, including its entire base, gills, odour and cut flesh. Discard uncertain or old specimens and obtain expert identification before eating wild mushrooms.

traits: White to creamy domed cap, generally 3–11 cm
Free gills pink when opened, then chocolate brown; dark brown spore print
Short pale stem with a fragile ring that may disappear
No volva; cut flesh and base do not stain bright yellow
Meadows, pastures and lawns, often in autumn
safetyNote: Edible only after certain identification of each specimen. White gills, a volva, bright yellow staining or a chemical odour are warning signs. Do not eat closed buttons whose diagnostic features cannot be seen; ask an expert when unsure.
